I have been farming in Quzhou for 40 years. At 55, I know what this land can do. With only two of us at home and some off-farm work to keep cash flowing, I cannot manage everything by hand. That is why I keep my wheat-maize rotation to 24 mu on the best-irrigated plot near the well — it gives me reliable grain, and the maize goes in right after wheat harvest in early June without missing a beat. I plant millet on 100 mu because it is drought-tolerant and low-labor; even with modest yields, 100 mu adds up to a solid harvest that does not need much watching. Cotton I keep to just 5 mu. The price is decent, but it is labor-intensive — too much spraying and picking for a household our size, so I grow only what I can manage.

For wheat, I rotary-till before sowing in October and use an improved variety at 30 jin per mu. I apply compound fertilizer as a basal dressing and topdress with urea at green-up — about 25 kg of nitrogen per mu in total. I irrigate three times: winter irrigation, green-up, and one at heading. I spray insecticide twice and herbicide once; after four decades I know the pest calendar here by heart.

For maize, I plant hybrid Denghai 605 immediately after wheat harvest without tilling. No-tillage saves fuel and time, and the wheat stubble helps hold moisture. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing, roughly 18 kg nitrogen per mu, and irrigate twice in summer when the well water is needed. I spray for weeds and pests three times total.

For cotton, I rotary-till in mid-April and sow an improved variety at 2.5 jin per mu. It demands attention — I irrigate twice and spray insecticide nine times plus herbicide once, because bollworm pressure is always heavy in this county. I apply about 15 kg nitrogen per mu.

For millet, I rotary-till and sow in early July with traditional seed at 2 jin per mu. It is the easiest crop I grow — one irrigation, one spray, and about 8 kg nitrogen per mu from compound fertilizer. It basically takes care of itself while I am busy with wheat, maize, and cotton.

I expect wheat to yield about 1,050 kg per mu, maize about 1,150 kg per mu, cotton about 600 kg per mu, and millet about 680 kg per mu — close to what I have achieved in recent years.
